opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's something we've thought about from day one, because the economics of serving models are quite different from the economics of training them. Training is a large upfront investment; serving is a recurring cost that grows with your usage, so if you don't get it right, success can actually hurt you.

There are a few layers to it. The first is the model itself. Our whole philosophy has been to make models that are as efficient as possible for a given level of performance: compressing as much knowledge as we can into fewer parameters, and using architectures like sparse mixture-of-experts, where you only activate part of the network for each token. That directly translates into lower inference cost, and that's the biggest lever you have, much bigger than anything you can do afterwards.

The second layer is the inference stack. That means good kernels, efficient batching, managing memory well, especially the KV cache when you have long contexts, quantization when it doesn't hurt quality, and things like speculative decoding. A lot of this is unglamorous engineering, but it compounds. Every percentage point of GPU utilization you gain matters when you run at scale.

The third layer is the infrastructure and the business side: how you schedule workloads, how you handle peaks versus off-peak usage, how you choose between hardware providers, and being able to deploy on different platforms, whether it's our own platform, the cloud providers, or on-premise for customers who want to run things themselves. Being portable gives you leverage and flexibility.

And finally there's a co-design aspect. The people training the models and the people serving them need to talk to each other constantly. If you design the model knowing how it's going to be served, you make better choices. That's something a relatively small, focused team can do well, because you don't have big walls between research and product.

Ultimately, the goal is that developers and enterprises get frontier-level performance at a price that makes sense for their use case, because a lot of the value of this technology only appears when it's cheap enough to use everywhere, not just in a few high-value applications.

r001.rationale: It identifies model-design choices—compressing knowledge into fewer parameters and using sparse mixture-of-experts—as major ways to reduce serving cost.

r002.rationale: It describes inference-stack work, including kernels, batching, memory management, quantization, and speculative decoding, alongside architectural efficiency as a further layer that compounds the gains.

fable-5.1.text:
So I think the first thing to say is that cost efficiency isn't a layer you add at the end. It starts at the model level. If you train a model that is dense and very large, there's a floor on serving cost that no amount of infrastructure work gets you below. That's a big part of why we've invested in mixture-of-experts architectures and in smaller models that punch above their weight. You want to get the most capability per active parameter, because every active parameter is compute you pay for on every token, forever.

Then there's the inference stack itself, and that's where a lot of the engineering goes. Batching is the obvious one. GPUs are only efficient when they're busy, so you want to be filling them with many requests at once, and continuous batching, where you're slotting new requests in as others finish, makes a big difference. Then KV cache management, because memory, not FLOPs, is usually the binding constraint on how many concurrent sequences you can serve. Quantization is another lever, going to lower precision for weights and sometimes activations without hurting quality. And speculative decoding, where a small draft model proposes tokens and the big model verifies them, which helps a lot with latency on long generations.

The thing people underestimate is that these are not independent. The choices you make in training, say the size of the attention heads or the vocabulary, show up directly in how well you can batch and how much cache you need. So we've tried to keep the training team and the inference team very close. When a model is being designed, the question "how will this serve?" is on the table from day one.

And then on the business side, open weights change the calculus. A lot of our customers deploy on their own infrastructure, so we're not always the ones paying the serving bill, but we are responsible for making the model efficient enough that they can. That discipline carries over to our own platform.

The last point is that we're a small team relative to the labs we compete with, so we can't afford to be wasteful. Efficiency isn't a nice-to-have for us. It's how we exist.

r001.rationale: The response identifies mixture-of-experts and smaller models as ways to reduce serving compute, but does not identify them as memory-efficient model architectures.

r002.rationale: The response says training choices affect batching and cache needs, and that the training and inference teams work closely so serving is considered during model design.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to look at the whole stack. The model itself matters a lot—how much computation it needs, how much memory it uses—but then there’s all the work around serving it: batching requests, managing the cache, and keeping the GPUs busy without making people wait too long.

And those things have to be designed together. A model that looks efficient in isolation may not be efficient under a real mix of customer requests. So the work is quite empirical: understand the workloads, measure where the bottlenecks are, and improve both the model and the serving system. The objective is to bring down the cost of delivering a useful answer at the quality and latency the application needs.

r001.rationale: It mentions the model’s computation and memory use, but does not identify training-time choices or memory-efficient architectures.

r002.rationale: It says model efficiency in isolation may not carry over to real workloads and that both the model and serving system must be improved, communicating the need for inference-side work to realize serving efficiency.

sol-6.1.text:
There’s a lot of work beyond training a good model. You need to make inference efficient, which means working on the kernels, on batching, on how you distribute the model across GPUs, and on keeping those GPUs busy. And those decisions depend on the workload: serving a lot of short requests is quite different from serving long contexts.

The advantage of building both the models and the serving platform is that we can optimize them together. We can make architectural choices with deployment in mind, then adapt the inference stack to those choices. Ultimately, what matters is the cost of delivering the quality and latency the customer needs, so you have to look at the whole system.

r001.rationale: The response mentions making architectural choices with deployment in mind, but does not identify training-time choices of memory-efficient architectures.

r002.rationale: It says inference must be made efficient and the inference stack adapted to the model’s architectural choices.
